Unit Summary

Part A established that learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour through experience, with three elements (process, effect, permanence) and six characteristics. Multiple internal and external factors influence learning, leading to twelve principles that guide effective practice.

Part B distinguished types of learning: rote (passive, dependent) versus meaningful (active, independent). Active learning involves doing AND thinking, with specific techniques like Think-Pair-Share, Socratic Method, and Fish Bowl. Self-learning represents the highest form — independent, lifelong, resourceful learning.

Part C showed that self-learning develops when learners have high motivation, confidence, and satisfaction from completing tasks. Twenty benefits include independent thinking, better retention, and preparation for lifelong learning.

Part D explained that teaching exists to facilitate learning. It is both art and science, with characteristics including being social, observable, and evaluable. Good teaching in a democratic society provides self-learning opportunities, addresses individual differences, creates warm environments, and uses both formative and summative assessment.

The connection: Everything flows from the core concept — learning is behaviour change through experience. Teaching creates those experiences. The best teaching develops self-directed, meaningful, active learners who can continue learning throughout life.

docs.title: Unit 2: Teaching in Diverse Classrooms and Learning In and Out of School
Introduction
docs.text:
This unit addresses two interconnected realities of education:

  1. Classrooms are diverse — students differ in abilities, backgrounds, and learning needs
  2. Learning extends beyond school — meaningful education happens in many settings

These concepts are connected: understanding diversity helps teachers see that different students may learn better in different environments. A child struggling in a traditional classroom might excel when learning through observation in a real-world setting. Together, these ideas shape how we design complete educational experiences.

docs.title: Part A: Teaching in Diverse Classrooms
2.01 Concept of Diversity
docs.text:
Diversity means a group with variety or dissimilar elements. The term is interpreted according to context:

Context What Diversity Means Social Diversity People in a community differ in caste, religion, race, language, locality, economic status, occupation Biodiversity Different organisms classified as plants, animals, insects, reptiles, birds based on physical forms Classroom Diversity Students differ in intelligence, language ability, interests, aptitudes, learning style, socio-economic status

Why this matters: Just as biodiversity makes ecosystems resilient, classroom diversity enriches the learning environment — but it also requires teachers to adapt their approaches.

docs.title: 2.02 Meaning and Definition of Diverse Classrooms
docs.text:
Students in any classroom differ in physical and psychological traits as well as behaviour:

  • Gifted children who grasp concepts quickly
  • Average learners who form the majority
  • Slow learners or those with learning disabilities
  • Students from marginalized sections (weaker sections, minority communities, tribals, scheduled castes)
  • Students from different castes, religions, and mother tongues

Definition

A Diverse Classroom is one in which students significantly differ in their physical and psychological traits, socio-economic status, and learning abilities. In such classrooms, teaching-learning activities must also be diverse.

The connection: Because students are diverse, teaching methods cannot be uniform. This leads directly to the concept of differentiated instruction discussed later.

docs.title: 2.03 Types of Diversity in Classrooms
docs.text: Some diversity is obvious (race, dress, language). Other diversity is invisible (learning styles, motivation, beliefs). A responsive teacher must recognize and provide for all types:

docs.title: 1. Student Background
docs.text:
India has many religions, castes, and languages. In classrooms, especially urban ones, you find:

  • Students with different mother tongues
  • Different religious practices (Muslim girls wearing purdah, turbaned Sikhs, caste marks)
  • Different dress styles (traditional sari, modern churidar, gowns)

docs.title: 2. Cognitive Ability
docs.text:
Students with high cognitive abilities sit beside slow learners. This creates a challenging teaching task because:

  • Grouping by ability level is one option
  • Individualized instruction suits different cognitive levels
  • Inclusive classrooms help slow learners but may concern parents of gifted children

docs.title: 3. Different Levels of Motivation
docs.text:
Motivation varies due to:

  • Family environment — problems at home affect concentration
  • Cognitive aptitude — low ability leads to dislike of assignments
  • Attitude toward school — students who feel mistreated show withdrawal tendency

Connection to learning: Low motivation directly affects learning achievement, which is why teachers must use reinforcement strategies (discussed in Section 2.06).

docs.title: 4. Learning Difficulties
docs.text:
Even students with average intelligence may have:

Learning Difficulty What It Affects Phonological disorder Speech Dyslexia Reading Dysgraphia Writing Dyscalculia Mathematical computation

These decrease learning interest and efficiency, requiring special attention (see Section 2.06:7).

docs.title: 5. Diversity in Faith and Ideas
docs.text:
Students have different religious beliefs and political thoughts. When teachers or peers impose ideas:

  • Conflict and confusion arise
  • Some students blindly support teachers to avoid displeasure
  • This affects personality development

Important: Teachers and students should mutually respect others' rights.

docs.title: 6. Diversity in Lifestyle
docs.text: Rural and urban students differ in habits and language command. They may not mix, remaining as separate islands, which affects learning achievement.

docs.title: 7. Awareness about Cultural Differences (Positive Attitude)
docs.text:
Diverse classrooms offer chances to interact with different backgrounds. This:

  • Widens viewpoints
  • Develops cultural awareness
  • Prevents racial, religious, and social abuses
  • Teaches acceptance and respect for other traditions

docs.title: 8. Tolerance and Acceptance
docs.text:
Working together in group activities develops:

  • Understanding of human diversities
  • Tolerance and adjustment skills
  • Ability to complete group assignments successfully

Key Insight

These eight types of diversity are interconnected. A student's background (Type 1) affects their motivation (Type 3). Learning difficulties (Type 4) interact with cognitive ability (Type 2). Cultural awareness (Type 7) enables tolerance (Type 8). Teachers must see the whole picture.

docs.title: 2.04 Teaching in a Diverse Classroom: Differentiated Instruction
docs.text:
In diverse classrooms, teachers must implement differentiated instruction — adapting teaching to fulfill learning needs of all students.

There are three important aspects:

Differentiated Instruction
         │
         ├── 1. Differentiating Content (What to learn)
         │
         ├── 2. Differentiating Process (How to learn)
         │
         └── 3. Differentiating Evaluation (How to assess)

docs.title: 2.04:1 Differentiating Content to be Learned
docs.text:
Content includes knowledge, concepts, practical skills, and positive attitudes from the curriculum.

Methods for differentiating content delivery:

  • Demonstration
  • Audio-visual aids
  • Lecturing and explaining
  • Discussion
  • Graphical representations

Why differentiate content? Students with different cognitive abilities (Type 2 diversity) and learning difficulties (Type 4) need information presented in different ways.

docs.title: 2.04:2 Differentiating Learning Processes
docs.text:
Learning process refers to how students understand and internalize content. Students need reflection before moving to the next segment.

Helpful learning activities:

Activity Purpose Workshop Hands-on practice and reflection Group Learning Collaboration and social skills Learning Resource Centers Extra support for challenged students

Learning Resource Centers

Physically challenged, mentally handicapped, and students with learning difficulties attend classroom instruction, then go to Learning Resource Centers on campus to strengthen learning with help from special education teachers.

Group learning with mixed boys and girls promotes:

  • Social skills
  • Harmonious behaviour
  • Understanding differences among people

Connection: This addresses the tolerance and acceptance (Type 8 diversity) — students learn to work with different people.

docs.title: 2.04:3 Using Different Methods for Evaluating Learning
docs.text:
Just as content and process are differentiated, evaluation methods must vary:

Traditional Methods Novel Methods Written tests Quiz programmes Examinations Objective/Multiple Choice tests Practical examinations Project work evaluation Assignment evaluation Pair and share technique

Pair and Share Technique

Each student evaluates the learning proficiency of their partner with whom they learned a task and shared experiences. Teacher compares student evaluation with their own to finalize assessment.

What gets evaluated: Not just subject content mastery, but also social skills, participation, and other aspects.

docs.title: 2.05 Preparation of Teachers for Diverse Classrooms
docs.text: How do teachers learn to handle diversity? Through systematic preparation:

docs.title: Stage 1: Micro-teaching
docs.text:
Develop individual teaching skills:

  • Set induction (introducing a topic)
  • Explaining
  • Questioning
  • Demonstration
  • Blackboard writing
  • Stimulus variation
  • Reinforcement
  • Closure

docs.title: Stage 2: Skill Integration
docs.text: Practice combining skills in full lessons through judicious selection.

docs.title: Stage 3: Peer Teaching and Feedback
docs.text:
• Observe peer teachings
  • Analyze them
  • Receive professor's feedback
  • Understand various teaching techniques

docs.title: Stage 4: Diverse Classroom Exposure
docs.text:
Visit different settings to understand diverse students:

Type of Institution What You Learn Government schools Students from weaker sections Special schools Deaf, dumb, visually handicapped students Schools for mentally challenged Different learning needs Residential schools Community living dynamics International schools Alternative teaching approaches

docs.title: Stage 5: Social Awareness Activities
docs.text:
Participate in activities during weekly holidays:

  • Visit slums and villages
  • Engage in literacy movements
  • Create health awareness
  • Promote nutritious food knowledge
  • Encourage personal hygiene

Connection: Understanding the backgrounds students come from (Type 1 diversity) helps teachers address motivation issues (Type 3) and lifestyle differences (Type 6).

docs.title: 2.06 Effective Teaching in a Diverse Classroom
docs.text: Eight dimensions of effective teaching address the challenges of diversity:

docs.title: 2.06:1 Simplify Content and Present Effectively
docs.text:
• Arrange concepts in logical order
  • Relate to students' prior knowledge
  • Use multimedia presentation because learning styles differ

Some students prefer: - Teacher explaining with examples - Visual presentation - Learning by doing - Individualized learning - Group learning

Connection to diversity: This addresses cognitive ability differences (Type 2) and learning difficulties (Type 4).

docs.title: 2.06:2 Give Due Importance to Group Work
docs.text:
For Mixed Ability Groups, avoid: - ✗ One teaching method for whole class - ✗ Teaching centered only on average learners - ✗ Teacher-centered interactions only

Use group-based techniques:

  1. Group Interactive Classroom Sessions
  2. Cooperative Learning
  3. Collaborative Learning
  4. Group Assignments
  5. Group Investigation Learning
  6. Group Project Work

Connection: Group work builds tolerance (Type 8) and addresses different motivation levels (Type 3).

docs.title: 2.06:3 Give More Scope for Student Interaction
docs.text:
Classroom activities fall under three categories:

Classroom Interactions
         │
         ├── Perception about classroom climate
         │
         ├── Diagnosis
         │
         └── Action-Reaction Process (most important)

Interaction types:

Verbal Interactions Non-Verbal Interactions Teacher initiates → Students respond Related to teaching task Students initiate → Teacher responds Not related to teaching task

Key principle: Student participation must be high for active learning.

docs.title: 2.06:4 Provide Immediate Feedback
docs.text:
When students complete any task (test, classroom answer, assignment, project), provide:

  • Whether task is done correctly or not
  • If correct, to what extent
  • If incorrect, why it is incorrect

Why immediate? Enables students to get motivated, continue learning, achieve mastery, and progress with enthusiasm.

docs.title: 2.06:5 Motivate Students to Actively Engage
docs.text:
Use reinforcement: - Praise correct responses - Reward achievement - Provide immediate feedback

Structure assignments strategically:

Difficulty Progression:
Easy (everyone can complete) → Gradually increasing → Difficult

NOT: Difficult first → Easy later

Principle: Initial success motivates students to try harder tasks. Success breeds success.

Connection: This directly addresses motivation differences (Type 3 diversity).

docs.title: 2.06:6 Relate Subject Content with Practical Life
docs.text:
Use examples from day-to-day life when explaining concepts:

  • All sections of students understand more easily
  • Interest in learning increases
  • Knowledge becomes meaningful

Connection to Part B: This principle connects to out-of-school learning — real-life applications show why learning beyond classroom matters.

docs.title: 2.06:7 Pay Special Attention to Students Who Lag Behind
docs.text:
Two methods to help struggling students:

Method Description Supervised Study Teacher monitors and guides while student works Tutorial Method One-on-one or small group focused teaching

docs.title: 2.06:8 Refer to Specialist Teachers
docs.text:
For disabled students, connect with itinerant teachers — specialists who visit schools regularly to support specific needs.

How the Eight Dimensions Connect

These dimensions form a system: Simplified content (1) allows group work (2) where interactions (3) occur. Immediate feedback (4) maintains motivation (5). Real-life connections (6) help all students. Special attention (7) and specialists (8) ensure no one is left behind.

docs.title: Part B: Learning In and Out of School
2.07 Concept of Out-of-School Learning
docs.text: The connection between diverse classrooms and out-of-school learning is this: students who struggle in traditional classrooms may learn better through direct experience in real settings.

docs.title: Historical Background
docs.text: Year Thinker Key Idea 1974 Ivan Illich "Deschooling Society" — questioned whether schools are the only way to learn 1974+ John Holt "Could schools alone serve as the best places to provide education? Or are there other alternatives?" 1987 Lauren Resnik Popularized out-of-school learning concept at Agricultural Economics Research Association

docs.title: What is Out-of-School Learning?
docs.text:
All experiences (academic and non-academic) that students get outside school:

Traditional community resources: - Hospitals, engineering industries, automobile repair shops - Zoo, botanical gardens, horticultural gardens - Hotels, tailoring shops, bakeries - Libraries, science museums, cine studios

Modern addition: Learning from home using electronic media, particularly internet (though some hesitate to include this since it's not in a social setting).

docs.title: 2.07:1 Salient Features of Out-of-School Learning
docs.text:
Feature Description Social settings Learning happens in community, not isolation Direct experiences Contact with objects and events in their own settings Unstructured but planned Flexible yet purposeful environments Collaboration Learning with others and sharing learning Observation emphasis Learning through watching Group assessment Achievement evaluated by group performance, not individual

Connection to diverse classrooms: Students with different learning styles (a hidden diversity) may thrive in these unstructured, observation-based, collaborative settings.

docs.title: 2.08 Purposes of Learning In and Out of School
2.08:1 Purposes of Learning IN School
docs.text:
Purpose What Students Develop Cognitive and physical skills Skills for successful daily life Higher-order abilities Inquiry, logical thinking, value analysis, problem-solving Cultural elements Language, social practices, values, knowledge, traditions, ethics, laws Good conduct Ethical behaviour and personal hygiene Vocational foundation Basic knowledge for self-reliance Citizenship Preparation for civic duties

Summary: School education blooms latent potential and develops personality through structured activities. It provides "what we know".

docs.title: 2.08:2 Purposes of Learning OUT OF School
docs.text:
Society continuously changes — dress habits, food, marriage rituals, production techniques, transport, communication (material culture) as well as language, customs, beliefs, attitudes, laws (non-material culture).

Key Insight

Teaching today's technology and lifestyles is insufficient because they will change. Instead, develop the ability to adapt to any change — this is true education.

What out-of-school learning provides:

What Students Gain How They Gain It Problem management ability Direct experience in society Social skills Collaborating and sharing with others Adaptation skills New situations in real settings Life skills and problem-solving Real-life situations

Summary: Out-of-school learning provides "what we need to know" — practical, adaptable knowledge.

docs.title: 2.08:3 Comparison: Learning In School vs. Out of School
docs.text:
Aspect In School Out of School Teacher's role Actively teaches, key role in learning Students take responsibility, learn through direct experience Evaluation focus Individual-centered activities and assessment Students share activities, work with team spirit Skills emphasis Intellectual and physical skills Higher-order mental skills PLUS social skills (collaboration, adjustment, adaptation) Knowledge type Theoretical Empirical and functional Retention May forget over time (except basic skills) Internalized through experience, not easily forgotten Scope of knowledge Wide but shallow (general skills) Narrow but deep (situation-specific skills) Adaptation Limited environmental adaptation Develops ability to adapt to new situations Learning activities Listening, seeing, reading; individual assessment Observation, personal handling, natural/social settings; group assessment

The Connection: Both are needed. School provides breadth and foundation; out-of-school provides depth and practical application.

docs.title: 2.09:1 Meaning of Observational Learning
docs.text:
Observational learning involves:

  1. Keenly watching how others perform a task
  2. Understanding components and their arrangement
  3. Remembering these details
  4. Trying the task repeatedly
  5. Eliminating errors
  6. Achieving similar performance

What it develops: - Language and physical skills - Moral behaviour - Social attitudes

Role Model and Modelling

The person we watch and try to imitate is our role model. Learning by observation is called modelling. Teachers and parents must behave as good role models.

docs.title: 2.09:1:01 Steps in Observational Learning (Bandura)
docs.text:
Step Process Description 1 Attending and Perceiving Child's attention is attracted by role model or demonstration 2 Remembering Child remembers actions and behaviour observed 3 Converting memory to action Child analyzes acceptability and imitates only relevant, acceptable elements 4 Reinforcement Only behaviours that receive appropriate feedback become fixed

Key insight: Children don't imitate everything — they select what seems relevant and acceptable. Reinforcement determines what sticks.

docs.title: 2.09:2 Importance in Out-of-School Learning
docs.text:
Why classroom learning is insufficient:

  • Cannot provide all information and practical uses
  • Functional knowledge requires natural and social environments
  • Practical skills need real settings

This is why educators like John Dewey advocated project work.

Applications:

Setting How Observational Learning Helps Vocational education Apprenticeship under professional experts/supervisors Fine arts academies Learning by watching master artists Technical training centers Observing experienced workers Personal interests Pursuing passions through observation Learning difficulties Alternative paths when classroom fails

Components of observational learning: - Observing objects, events, acts in natural settings - Gathering appropriate information - Interpreting collected data - Analyzing, classifying, synthesizing

In apprenticeship: - Observe efficient workers - Identify components and sequence - Note perfection achieved - Retain in memory - Try performing - Receive supervisor feedback - Practice until errors disappear and speed increases

docs.title: 2.10 Approaches to Learning Outside the Classroom
2.10:1 Modern View
docs.text:
Traditional view: Learn in social settings using community resources (hospitals, gardens, museums, workshops, etc.)

Modern view: Internet-based learning from home. Access any website to learn about: - Preparing food recipes - Yoga, music, dance - Science experiments - Machine assembly and repair - World parks and famous buildings - Archaeological findings - Space research

Three approaches to out-of-school learning:

Out-of-School Learning Approaches
              │
              ├── 1. Field Training (Field Trip)
              │
              ├── 2. Field Research
              │
              └── 3. Web-based Learning

docs.title: 2.10:2 Field Training (Field Trip)
docs.text:
Definition: Training designed for students to get full sensory experiences with things and phenomena that cannot be brought into the classroom.

Three Phases:

Phase Activities Pre-field Teacher outlines key concepts, asks students to study topic, displays related video/slides Field Work Make arrangements, reach location, give directions about what to observe and record, students collect information and interpretations Post-field Discussion of observations, individual reports (diagrams, stories, poems, essays), teacher evaluation and feedback

Benefits: - Students report observations with their own interpretations - Even students without personal experience learn from shared notes - Direct experiences through structured situations

Using Field Trip as Teaching Aid:

  1. Preview the place after determining purpose
  2. Make arrangements with school and site authorities
  3. Prepare pupils physically and mentally — make trip feel essential and interesting, clarify what to look for
  4. Function as prudent guide — allow students to observe, take notes, draw sketches, collect materials
  5. Follow-up work — discussions, readings, exhibitions, laboratory verification
  6. Evaluate in terms of specific educational gains

docs.title: 2.10:3 Field Research
docs.text:
Steps involved:

Step Activity 1. Sensing the Problem From teacher explanation, personal observation, or interest, select problem for solution 2. Formulating Hypothesis Through critical thinking, reading, discussion, propose possible solution statement 3. Field Activities Collect required data to test hypothesis 4. Data Analysis Process raw data, classify, tabulate, make statistical analysis 5. Hypothesis Testing Accept or reject hypothesis based on findings 6. Write-up Prepare short report of problem-solving method

Methods used: Inductive and deductive reasoning

Skills developed: Observation, information collection, description, explanation — all centered on problem-solving using scientific method.

Connection: Field research applies the problem-solving skills that school develops, in real-world settings.

docs.title: 2.10:4 Learning Through Websites
docs.text:
Steps involved:

Step Activity 1 Search websites using search engines (Google) 2 Select appropriate websites, surf using browser 3 Find relevant information, download and store as file 4 Print out; share via email if needed 5 Process, arrange sequentially, prepare report with text and pictures

docs.title: 2.11 Advantages of Learning Outside the Classroom
2.11:1 Advantages of Field Trip and Field Research
docs.text:
1. First-hand quality experiences — natural phenomena in proper background
  2. Close contact with environment
  3. Develops observation and reasoning skills
  4. Encourages active learning
  5. Socializes school activities — school and community get closer
  6. Materials collection for school museum/exhibition
  7. Develops social skills
  8. Opportunities for collaborative learning and sharing
  9. Makes knowledge meaningful and enlarges it
  10. Develops problem-solving skills

docs.title: 2.11:2 Advantages of Web-based Learning
docs.text:
1. Develops ability to derive meaning and engage in active discourse
  2. Encourages self-construction of knowledge instead of receiving tailor-made information
  3. Enables mutual sharing between teacher and students
  4. Learner-centred
  5. Encourages active participation and knowledge construction
  6. Fosters higher-order cognitive abilities — analysis, synthesis, evaluation
  7. Encourages active learning
  8. Allows group learning — develops cooperation and understanding
  9. Enables interaction at different levels
  10. Focuses on real-world events and problem-solving

docs.title: 2.12 Limitations of Learning Outside the Classroom
Challenges in Field Trips and Field Research
docs.text: Challenge Description Supervision Large numbers of students need help Scheduling Difficulty framing time table Missed lessons Hard to arrange make-up sessions Logistics Challenging to arrange and conduct Cost Travel and stay expenses Knowledge gaps May not know enough about field location Safety Ensuring student safety Skill gaps Most students lack ability to collect and interpret information Attitude Danger of treating trip as excursion/pleasure tour

docs.title: Challenges in Web-based Learning
docs.text:
Challenge Description Computer skills Students may lack ability to operate computers, search, collect information Language barrier About 90% of web information is in English — challenging for rural students Interpretation Lack ability to properly interpret and select from collected materials Technical skills Cannot download and record to compact discs Access Not all students have computer and internet Reporting Cannot process, arrange logically, and prepare written reports

Reality in India

Language skills, computer skills, information selection and interpretation, logical arrangement and report writing — adequate practice and proficiency may be lacking in Indian students. This makes 'learning outside school' techniques appear as a rare feat.

docs.title: The Connection Between Parts A and B
docs.text:
DIVERSE CLASSROOMS (Part A)          OUT-OF-SCHOOL LEARNING (Part B)
         │                                        │
         │ Students differ in:                    │ Learning happens through:
         │ • Cognitive ability                    │ • Observation
         │ • Motivation                           │ • Field experience
         │ • Learning style                       │ • Research
         │ • Background                           │ • Web resources
         │                                        │
         └──────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                        │
                        ▼
              EFFECTIVE TEACHING
                        │
         ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
         │                             │
    Differentiated              Multiple Learning
    Instruction                 Environments
         │                             │
         └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                        │
                        ▼
              EVERY STUDENT LEARNS

The key insight: Diversity means students learn differently. Out-of-school learning provides alternative pathways. Together, differentiated instruction and multiple environments ensure all students can succeed.

docs.title: Remembering (C - Concept)
docs.text:
1. What do you mean by 'Diversity'? [Ans: 2.01]
  2. What is the meaning of 'Diverse Classroom'? [Ans: 2.02]
  3. State the salient features of out-of-school learning. [Ans: 2.07:1]
  4. What are the purposes of learning in school? [Ans: 2.08:1]

docs.title: Understanding (B - Basic Application)
docs.text:
1. Explain the concept of "Out-of-School Learning". [Ans: 2.07]
  2. Explain the purposes of learning outside school. [Ans: 2.08:2]
  3. Clarify the modern view about out-of-school learning. [Ans: 2.10:1]

docs.title: Applying/Analyzing (A - Advanced)
docs.text:
1. Explain the reasons for diversity in the classroom OR State the various types of diversity. [Ans: 2.03]

  2. Discuss the important aspects of teaching in a diverse classroom. [Ans: 2.04 + 2.04:1 to 2.04:3]

  3. Explain preparing teachers for diverse classrooms. [Ans: 2.05]

  4. Discuss dimensions of effective teaching in diverse classrooms. [Ans: 2.06 + 2.06:1 to 2.06:7]

  5. Compare learning in school with learning out of school. [Ans: 2.07 + 2.07:1 + 2.08:1 to 2.08:3]

  6. What is Observational Learning? Explain steps and importance in out-of-school learning. [Ans: 2.09:1 + 2.09:1:01 + 2.09:2]

  7. Discuss two approaches of out-of-school learning. [Ans: 2.10 + 2.10:1 + 2.10:2 + 2.10:2:01 + 2.10:3]

  8. Explain out-of-school learning concept and discuss advantages and limitations. [Ans: 2.10:1 + 2.11 + 2.11:1 + 2.11:2 + 2.12]

Unit Summary

Part A established that classrooms contain students with eight types of diversity (background, cognitive ability, motivation, learning difficulties, faith/ideas, lifestyle, cultural awareness, tolerance). To address this, teachers use differentiated instruction across content, process, and evaluation. Effective teaching involves eight dimensions from simplifying content to using specialists.

Part B showed that learning extends beyond school walls. Out-of-school learning provides direct experience, observation-based learning, and social skills that complement school's theoretical foundation. Observational learning (Bandura's four steps) enables learning through role models. Three approaches — field trips, field research, and web-based learning — each have specific advantages and limitations.

The connection: Diverse students need diverse learning environments. Combining differentiated classroom instruction with meaningful out-of-school experiences ensures every student can learn effectively.

docs.title: Unit III: Theory of Constructivism and Learner-Centered Teaching
🎯 Unit Overview: The Big Picture
docs.text:
This unit explores two interconnected revolutionary ideas that transformed education in the 20th century:

flowchart TD
    A[Traditional View: Learning = Receiving Information] -->|Challenged by| B[Constructivism]
    B -->|Led to| C[Learner-Centered Teaching]
    B -->|Key Idea| D[Students BUILD their own knowledge]
    C -->|Key Idea| E[Teaching focuses on STUDENT needs]
    D --> F[Better Understanding & Retention]
    E --> F

docs.title: The Core Connection
docs.text: Old View New View (This Unit) Teacher gives knowledge → Student receives it Student constructs knowledge with teacher's guidance Teacher is the center Learner is the center Passive listening Active participation Memorization Meaningful understanding

docs.title: 3:00 Introduction
docs.text:
In the latter half of the 20th century, psychologists like Vygotsky, Piaget, Bruner, and Ausubel proposed a revolutionary view of learning called constructivism.

The Revolutionary Insight

Learning is NOT simply receiving information from a teacher. Instead, it's a process where learners:

  1. Examine new information
  2. Use their personal experiences to make sense of it
  3. Internalize and integrate it with their existing knowledge

This led to a parallel movement: Learner-Centered Teaching, which insists that all aspects of teaching—planning, execution, and evaluation—should be student-centered, not teacher-centered or subject-centered.

docs.title: Part 1: Constructivism - How Students Build Knowledge
The Process Explained
docs.text:
When you learn something new, here's what actually happens:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    YOUR EXISTING KNOWLEDGE                   │
│    (Built from your experiences, culture, background)        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ⬇️
              New Information Arrives (from teacher, book, etc.)
                              ⬇️
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    PROCESSING STAGE                          │
│  • Compare with existing knowledge                           │
│  • Find connections and meaning                              │
│  • Accept, modify, or reject based on experiences            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ⬇️
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    NEW UNDERSTANDING                         │
│    (Integrated with your existing cognitive structure)       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Key Definition

Learning (Constructivism) = The process of making information meaningful in the background of one's social and cultural environment and registering it in memory.

docs.title: What Learning is NOT
docs.text:
• ❌ Simply copying information received from outside
  • ❌ Just seeing, hearing, or reading and memorizing
  • ❌ Passively receiving knowledge from a teacher

docs.title: What Learning IS
docs.text:
• ✅ Making received information meaningful
  • ✅ Assimilating new information with existing knowledge
  • ✅ Constructing your own understanding

docs.title: The Teacher's New Role
docs.text:
In constructivism, the teacher is NOT a "dispenser of knowledge" but rather:

Role Description Cognitive Guide Helps students interact meaningfully with content Facilitator Creates suitable educational and social environment Co-Explorer Learns alongside students

docs.title: The Ideal Constructivist Classroom
docs.text:
• Students question, challenge, and formulate their own ideas
  • Active engagement, inquiry, and problem-solving are emphasized
  • Collaboration with others is encouraged
  • Single "correct answers" are de-emphasized

docs.title: 3:02 Definitions of Constructivism
docs.text: Scholar Definition Cannella & Reiff (1944) "Constructivism is an epistemology, a learning or meaning-making theory... individuals create or construct their own understandings or knowledge through the interactions and activities with which they have contact." Kroll & Boskey (1996) "Knowledge is acquired through involvement with content instead of imitation or repetition." Wolffe & McMullen (1996) "Constructivism is primarily a theory of learning, not a theory of teaching."

docs.title: 3:03 Nature of the Constructivist Learner
docs.text: Understanding the six characteristics of a constructivist learner:

docs.title: 1. 🎯 Full Responsibility for Learning
docs.text:
• Understanding comes from direct experiences
  • Active participation in learning activities is essential
  • The learner owns their learning journey

docs.title: 2. 💪 Self-Motivation is Essential
docs.text: "Only those who have confidence in their ability to learn are motivated to continuously involve themselves in learning activities." — Van Glaserfield (1989)

docs.title: 3. 🏃 Active Involvement
docs.text:
Learning occurs through:

  • Interaction with teacher and students
  • Working together with others
  • Searching for answers through inquiry
  • Reflecting upon experiences

docs.title: 4. 🤝 Collaboration with Peers
docs.text:
Why peer collaboration matters:

  • Share different experiences and perspectives
  • See possible interpretations from different angles
  • Achieve complete interpretation of what is learned

docs.title: 5. 🔍 Adopting an Inquiry Approach
docs.text:
The constructivist classroom provides opportunities for:

  • Problem-solving
  • Questioning
  • Accessing variety of sources
  • Critically analyzing information
  • Testing solutions through personal experience

Critical Thinking Required

Don't accept solutions offered by others blindly—test them and accept their validity through personal experiences.

docs.title: 6. 🪞 Reflecting on Learning Experiences
docs.text:
Reflection is crucial because:

  • Direct experience alone is not enough
  • Must select appropriate information
  • Must integrate with existing knowledge
  • Requires reflective and logical thinking capabilities

docs.title: 3:04 Role and Functions of Teacher in the Constructivist Classroom
docs.text: The teacher in a constructivist classroom:

docs.title: General Functions
docs.text: Function Description Ask open-ended questions Wait patiently for students to answer Emphasize higher-order thinking Focus on logical reasoning Encourage interaction Students interact with each other and teacher Promote experience sharing Students share among themselves Emphasize inquiry-based learning Learning through investigation Focus on problem-solving Real-world problem approaches Use collaborative techniques Group interactions, cooperative learning, jigsaw puzzles, project work

docs.title: The Four Phases of Cooperative Learning
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Phase 1: Pre-Lesson Decisions] --> B[Phase 2: Setting Tasks]
    B --> C[Phase 3: Monitoring Groups]
    C --> D[Phase 4: Evaluating Work]

docs.title: 3:04:1 Phase 1: Making Decisions Before the Lesson
docs.text:
Teacher decides on two types of objectives:

Objective Type Description Academic Objectives Content knowledge and skills for the lesson Social Objectives Social interaction skills to be acquired

docs.title: 3:04:2 Phase 2: Setting the Learning Tasks
docs.text:
• Explain learning tasks to student groups
  • Ensure students understand the tasks
  • Emphasize both academic AND social skill development

docs.title: 3:04:3 Phase 3: Monitoring and Intervening During Group Work
docs.text:
• Visit all groups during activities
  • Assess learning progress
  • Provide suggestions/assistance to lagging groups
  • Stimulate groups to accomplish assigned tasks

docs.title: 3:04:4 Phase 4: Evaluating the Product and Process
docs.text:
• Allow groups to assess their own achievement
  • Allow groups to assess other groups
  • Evaluate both lesson objectives AND social skills development

docs.title: 3:05 The Learning Process According to Constructivist Theory
Where Learning Happens: Working Memory
docs.text:
Knowledge construction occurs in short-term (working) memory through this process:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     LONG-TERM MEMORY                              │
│                   (Prior Knowledge Store)                         │
│           Audio Images 🔊    Visual Images 👁️                     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ⬆️ Select relevant prior knowledge
                              │
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    SHORT-TERM (WORKING) MEMORY                    │
│                                                                   │
│   Step 1: SELECTING                                               │
│   • Select from incoming information                              │
│   • Select from prior knowledge                                   │
│   • Compare and interpret meaningfully                            │
│                              ⬇️                                    │
│   Step 2: ORGANIZING                                              │
│   • Classify new information                                      │
│   • Code as audio/video images                                    │
│                              ⬇️                                    │
│   Step 3: INTEGRATING                                             │
│   • Combine organized new knowledge with existing knowledge       │
│   • Modify cognitive structure                                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ⬇️
                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │   NEW LEARNING   │
                    │    ACHIEVED!     │
                    └─────────────────┘

SOI Model

This three-step process is called the SOI Model:

  • S = Selecting
  • O = Organizing
  • I = Integrating

docs.title: 3:06 Pedagogical Approaches to Constructivism
docs.text: Four key teaching principles for constructivist classrooms:

docs.title: Principle 1: Connect New Learning to Prior Knowledge
docs.text:
"Learning is the process of connecting what we learn now, with what we already know."

For Teachers:

  • Test students' prior knowledge before teaching
  • Plan activities that help students connect new content to existing knowledge
  • Remember: Prior knowledge can facilitate, inhibit, or transform learning

docs.title: Principle 2: Relate Content to Real Life
docs.text:
• Present content related to students' day-to-day life
  • Don't assume students will discover everything themselves
  • Let students test what they learn in practical situations
  • Help students understand content as the teacher intended

docs.title: Principle 3: Use Social and Cultural Context
docs.text:
• Make students realize how they interpreted content in their social/cultural context
  • Encourage direct participation in social activities
  • Promote collaborative learning

docs.title: Principle 4: Develop Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK)
docs.text:
What is PCK?

A combination of:

  • Subject content knowledge
  • Teaching practice experience
  • Feedback from professors during training
  • Personal schooling experiences
  • Teaching experience in professional tenure

A Good Teacher

A good teacher has:

  1. Good understanding of subject content
  2. Skills for effective delivery
  3. Knowledge of students' abilities and backgrounds

docs.title: 3:07 Learning Environment That Facilitates Constructivism
docs.text:
According to Jonassen (1994), eight characteristics differentiate constructivist learning environments:

# Characteristic Meaning 1 Multiple representations of reality Show concepts from different angles 2 Avoid oversimplification Represent the complexity of the real world 3 Knowledge construction over reproduction Build understanding, don't just copy 4 Authentic tasks in meaningful context Real-world relevance, not abstract instruction 5 Real-world settings or case-based learning Not predetermined sequences of instruction 6 Encourage thoughtful reflection Think about experiences 7 Context and content dependent knowledge Learning depends on situation 8 Collaborative construction through social negotiation Work together, not compete

Teaching Methods Based on Constructivism:

  • Discovery learning
  • Hands-on experience
  • Experimental learning
  • Collaborative learning
  • Project-based learning
  • Task-based learning

docs.title: Part 2: Learner-Centered Teaching - Putting Students First
3:08 What is Learner-Centered Teaching?
docs.text:
Definition

Learner-Centered Teaching = Classroom teaching-learning activities arranged to maximize students' participation, taking into account their age, maturity level, and life environment.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Maximum active participation of students
  • Maximum classroom interactions
  • Prominent group work and collaborative learning
  • Content related to students' life environment

docs.title: Student-Centered Teaching Techniques
docs.text: Technique Description Debate Students argue different positions Seminar Student-led presentations and discussions Project-based method Long-term, real-world projects Field trip Learning outside the classroom Problem-solving method Students solve authentic problems Brain storming Generating many ideas quickly Colloquium Academic discussion sessions Keller Plan Self-paced, mastery-based learning Computer Assisted Instruction Technology-enhanced learning

docs.title: 1. Catering to Multiple Learning Styles
docs.text:
Students learn differently:

Learning Style Teaching Activity Visual learners Demonstrations, models Auditory learners Lectures, discussions Kinesthetic learners Hands-on assignments, projects Individual learners Library work, independent study Social learners Group discussions, field work

docs.title: 2. Promoting Learning Skills in Students
docs.text:
Just as teachers develop teaching skills, students develop:

  • Reflecting skills
  • Problem-solving skills
  • Evaluating with evidence
  • Forming hypotheses
  • Analyzing arguments
  • Reading comprehension

docs.title: 3. Emphasizing Group Learning
docs.text:
Methods that promote group learning:

  • Project method
  • Debate
  • Seminar
  • Brain-storming
  • Cooperative Learning
  • Collaborative Learning
  • Group Discussion

docs.title: 4. Using Students' Prior Knowledge Effectively
docs.text:
• Help students reconstruct their knowledge
  • Connect prior knowledge and experiences to new information

docs.title: 5. Making Learning Goals Transparent
docs.text:
• Students know what they will learn
  • Students know how they will assess their own learning

docs.title: 6. Promoting Enthusiastic Involvement
docs.text:
• Activities organized for active engagement
  • Students involve themselves willingly

docs.title: 7. Facilitating Self-Directed Learning
docs.text:
• Students learn by themselves
  • Students evaluate their own work
  • Students direct their own learning

docs.title: 3:10 Need for Learner-Centered Approaches
docs.text: The American Psychological Association identified five domains explaining why student-centered teaching is necessary:

docs.title: Domain 1: Developing Knowledge Base
docs.text:
"What a person already knows serves as the 'data base' for acquiring further knowledge." — Alexander & Murphy (2000)

Prior knowledge determines:

  • What new information we attend to
  • How we organize new information
  • How we filter new experiences
  • What we consider important or relevant

docs.title: Domain 2: Strategic Processing and Executive Control
docs.text:
Successful students:

  • Monitor their thinking
  • Reflect on their learning
  • Assume responsibility for their learning

"The ability to reflect on and regulate one's thoughts and behaviours is an essential aspect of learning." — Lambert & McCombs (2000)

docs.title: Domain 3: Motivation and Affect
docs.text:
Student-centered teaching increases:

  • Motivation for learning
  • Mental satisfaction in school activities
  • Personal involvement in learning
  • Intrinsic motivation
  • Confidence in abilities to succeed
  • Sense of control over learning

These lead to higher scholastic achievement.

docs.title: Domain 4: Individual Development and Differences
docs.text:
Why one-size-fits-all teaching doesn't work:

  • Students differ in cognitive ability
  • Students differ in capabilities
  • Students differ in prior experiences
  • Students differ in learning styles
  • Development is influenced by heredity AND environment

docs.title: Domain 5: Influence of Social Environment
docs.text:
Research by Bruner (1966), Piaget (1963), and Vygotsky (1978) highlights:

"Learning is a social process; so how a teacher teaches and how students are actively engaged in the process of learning determine what and how much they learn." — Lambert & McCombs (2000)

Collaborative learning techniques are highly effective in producing higher learning achievement.

docs.title: Summary: Why Student-Centered Learning is Necessary
docs.text:
mindmap
  root((Student-Centered Learning))
    Individual Differences
      Cognitive abilities
      Learning styles
      Prior experiences
    Knowledge Construction
      Real learning
      Meaningful understanding
    Student Involvement

docs.title: 3:11:1 Teacher-Centered Teaching
docs.text:
What it looks like:

  • Teacher functions actively, presents subject matter
  • Students sit passively, listen attentively
  • One-way communication (teacher → students)
  • Students work individually
  • Evaluation through objective tests and examinations

Based on the theory: "Learning is receiving subject content, internalizing it, and retrieving when required."

Examples: Lecture method, team teaching, classroom discussion, demonstration

docs.title: 3:11:1:01 Advantages of Teacher-Centered Teaching
docs.text: # Advantage 1 Classroom is quiet and orderly; teacher has full control 2 Teacher can monitor and control teaching-learning activities 3 Effective for lower-order cognitive objectives (knowing, understanding) 4 More time for teaching; students learn more content 5 Teacher with limited resources can teach large content to many students 6 Flexible—teacher can plan based on subject needs, student level, available resources 7 Teacher can use storytelling, analogies, demonstrations, questioning 8 Teacher can use verbal (praising) and non-verbal (gestures) reinforcers 9 Enables continuity and logical method 10 Teacher's charismatic personality stimulates enthusiastic learning

docs.title: 3:11:1:02 Limitations of Teacher-Centered Teaching
docs.text: # Limitation 1 No care for individual needs, interests, abilities, aptitude 2 Gap between what teacher stated and what students understood 3 Does not develop exploring, discovering, and self-initiative skills 4 Students become bored from passive listening 5 No collaboration skills developed; communication skills affected 6 Students cannot freely express views or ask questions 7 Based on memory; does not promote higher-order skills 8 Mismatch between teacher's presentation speed and students' understanding speed 9 One-way communication causes lack of interest

docs.title: 3:11:2 Student-Centered Teaching
docs.text:
What it looks like:

  • Both students and teachers play important roles
  • More interaction between teacher and students
  • Students exchange information and collaborate
  • Active participation in learning activities

docs.title: 3:11:2:02 Merits of Student-Centered Teaching
docs.text: # Merit 1 Students learn social skills (communication, collaboration) alongside academic skills 2 Students learn to regulate their learning, ask questions, collect information, act with self-reliance 3 Students enthusiastically involve themselves due to interaction opportunities 4 Knowledge is functional in nature—continuously renewed cognitive structure

docs.title: 3:11:2:03 Limitations of Student-Centered Teaching
docs.text: # Limitation 1 Classroom can become noisy and chaotic 2 Difficult for teacher to monitor all student activities 3 Some students may miss important ideas 4 Students who prefer independent work may struggle with group activities

docs.title: 3:11:3 Comparison Table
docs.text: # Aspect Teacher-Centered Student-Centered 1 Center of attention Teacher Teacher and students equally 2 Language focus Teacher's fluency Students' language skill 3 Student activity Sit passively, listen Interact with each other and teacher 4 Work arrangement Individual Pairs, groups, or individual (based on activity) 5 Monitoring Teacher monitors and corrects constantly Students discuss among themselves; teacher provides feedback when needed 6 Answering questions Teacher answers Students try to answer each other 7 Topic selection Teacher selects Students have opportunity to express views on topics 8 Evaluation Teacher evaluates students Students self-evaluate; teacher also evaluates 9 Classroom atmosphere Silent Often noisy and busy 10 Motivation Extrinsic (external rewards) Intrinsic (internal drive) 11 Communication One-way (teacher → students) Two-way (teacher ↔ students ↔ students) 12 Individual differences Not considered Fully considered 13 Thinking development Does not develop original thinking Nurtures original thinking, creativity, self-initiative 14 Understanding Possible gap between teaching and understanding Students interpret using prior knowledge 15 Skills emphasis Academic skills only Academic + social skills 16 Content quantity More content, shorter time Less content, but highly functional and practical

docs.title: 🎯 The Best Approach: Combining Both Methods
docs.text:
Practical Wisdom

Most effective teachers combine both methods:

  • Avoid the boredom of purely teacher-centered teaching
  • Avoid the wandering from goals in purely student-centered teaching
  • Students benefit from the strengths of both approaches

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This unit explores Teaching Models - systematic frameworks that guide teachers in creating effective learning environments. Think of a teaching model as a blueprint for instruction, similar to how an architect uses blueprints to construct buildings.

What You'll Learn

  • What teaching models are and why they matter
  • The six fundamental elements present in all teaching models
  • Three major categories: Philosophical, Psychological, and Modern models
  • How to apply these models in real classroom situations

docs.title: Understanding the Concept
docs.text:
The word "model" has several meanings in everyday life:

  1. Miniature representation - Like a model of the Taj Mahal
  2. Ideal figure for imitation - Like role models we look up to
  3. Professional blueprint - Like drawings used by architects and engineers

In education, a Teaching Model combines all these meanings - it's a detailed description of an ideal classroom environment designed to achieve specific learning objectives.

docs.title: Key Definitions
docs.text:
Scholar Definition Joyce & Weil (1972) "Teaching models are instructional designs that describe the process of specifying and producing particular environmental situations which cause students to interact in such a way that specific change occurs in their behaviour." Joyce & Weil "A pattern or plan which can be used to shape a curriculum, select instructional materials, and guide a teacher's actions." Paul D. Eggen (1979) "A teaching strategy to achieve instructional objectives, consisting of guidelines for designing educational activities and environments." Jangira (1983) "A set of interrelated components arranged in a sequence which provides guidelines to realize specific goals."

In Simple Terms

A Teaching Model describes the ways and means of creating a favorable environmental condition to promote desirable teacher-pupil interactions that bring desirable behaviour modification in students.

docs.title: 4.02 Characteristics of Teaching Models
docs.text:
All effective teaching models share these five key characteristics:

graph TD
    A[Teaching Model Characteristics] --> B[1. Scientific Procedure]
    A --> C[2. Specification of Learning Outcomes]
    A --> D[3. Specification of Environment]
    A --> E[4. Criterion of Performance]
    A --> F[5. Specification of Operations]

docs.title: 1. Scientific Procedure
docs.text:
• Not a haphazard combination of facts
  • A systematic procedure to modify learner behaviour
  • Based on clear assumptions and principles

docs.title: 2. Specification of Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
• Clearly defines expected performance after instruction
  • Details what students should be able to do upon completion

docs.title: 3. Specification of Environment
docs.text:
• Defines the conditions under which learning occurs
  • Describes circumstances for observing student responses

docs.title: 4. Criterion of Performance
docs.text:
• Sets the standard for acceptable student performance
  • Provides benchmarks for success

docs.title: 5. Specification of Operations
docs.text:
• Describes mechanisms for student-environment interaction
  • Outlines how students will engage with content

Why This Matters

A teaching model works like a blueprint for engineers - it saves energy, time, and effort while ensuring optimal use of available resources in the teaching-learning process.

docs.title: 4.03 Functions of a Teaching Model
docs.text:
A teaching model serves three essential functions:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    TEACHING MODEL                           │
├─────────────────┬─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┤
│   Function 1    │     Function 2      │     Function 3      │
├─────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
│ Designing &     │ Developing &        │ Specifying the      │
│ specifying      │ selecting           │ teaching-learning   │
│ instructional   │ instructional       │ activities          │
│ objectives      │ materials           │                     │
└─────────────────┴─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┘

docs.title: 4.04 Six Fundamental Elements of Teaching Models
docs.text: Every teaching model can be analyzed through these six basic elements:

docs.title: 4.04.1 Focus
docs.text:
• The central theme or aspect emphasized in the model
  • Includes teaching objectives and aspects of the teaching environment
  • What the model primarily aims to achieve

docs.title: 4.04.2 Syntax
docs.text:
• The sequential structure of teaching activities
  • Shows how to begin instruction and proceed further
  • Describes the internal organization and inter-relationships of activities

Think of it as...

Syntax is like a recipe's step-by-step instructions - it tells you the order of actions to follow.

docs.title: 4.04.3 Principles of Reactions
docs.text:
• Guidelines for how teachers should respond to student activities
  • Rules for selecting appropriate responses
  • Ensures responses are purposeful and selective

docs.title: 4.04.4 Social System
docs.text:
This covers three important aspects:

Aspect Description Classroom Climate Autocratic, Democratic, or Laissez-faire Role Definition Teacher and student roles (Active or Passive) Motivation Type Extrinsic, Intrinsic, or Self-motivation

docs.title: 4.04.5 Support System
docs.text:
Two key components:

  1. Instructional Resources
  2. Teaching aids (Audio-Visual aids)
  3. Facilities (Library, Laboratory, Workshops)

  4. Field trips and additional materials

  5. Evaluation Methods

  6. Testing devices to assess learning outcomes
  7. Methods for measuring teaching effectiveness

docs.title: 4.04.6 Application
docs.text:
• Specifies when and where to use a particular model
  • Depends on:
  • Kind of instructional objectives
  • Nature of subject matter
  • Teaching-learning situation

docs.title: 4.05 Classification of Teaching Models
docs.text:
Teaching models are classified into three broad categories:

                    TEACHING MODELS
                          │
        ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
        ▼                 ▼                 ▼
   PHILOSOPHICAL     PSYCHOLOGICAL        MODERN
        │                 │                 │
   ├── Locke's       ├── Glaser's      ├── Information
   │   Impression    │   Basic Model   │   Processing
   │   Model         │                 │   
   ├── Plato's       ├── Flander's     ├── Social
   │   Insight       │   Interaction   │   Interaction
   │   Model         │   Model         │
   │                 │                 ├── Personal
   └── Kant's        └── Davies &      │   Development
       Rule Model        Stolurow's    │
                         Computer      └── Behaviour
                         Model             Modification

docs.title: 4.06 Philosophical Teaching Models
docs.text: These models are rooted in philosophical traditions about how knowledge is acquired and understanding develops.

docs.title: 4.06.1 John Locke's Impression Model
docs.text:
About John Locke (1632-1704)

  • Born in Wrington, Somerset, England
  • Oxford scholar, economist, physician, and political philosopher
  • Believed in protecting natural rights: life, liberty, and property
  • A key figure among liberal philosophers

docs.title: Core Philosophy: Tabula Rasa
docs.text:
Locke believed children are born with their minds like a "blank slate" (tabula rasa). Educational experiences are recorded in the brain as impressions.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              LOCKE'S IMPRESSION MODEL               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                     │
│   Child's Mind (Blank Slate)                        │
│            ↓                                        │
│   Sensory Experiences (sight, hearing, smell, touch)│
│            ↓                                        │
│   Perceptual Images stored in mind                  │
│            ↓                                        │
│   Teacher explains with illustrations               │
│            ↓                                        │
│   Understanding and Learning                        │
│                                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Key Teaching Strategies
docs.text: Strategy Purpose Using simple teaching aids Provide sensory experiences Explaining with illustrations Make content understandable Asking questions Check understanding Summarising and reviewing Reinforce learning Writing on blackboard Visual reinforcement End-of-lesson assessment Evaluate learning achievement

docs.title: Connection to Other Models
docs.text:
Locke's Model Component Glaser's Model Equivalent Preparing students for learning Entry Behaviour Presentation, Correlation, Generalization Teaching Process Application Evaluation

Teacher's Role

In Locke's model, the teacher is highly active - simplifying content, presenting it in easy-to-understand ways, and using audio-visual aids to enhance learning interest.

docs.title: 4.06.2 Plato's Insight Model (Dialectical Method)
docs.text:
About Plato (424-423 BCE)

  • Born in Athens, ancient Greece, to an aristocratic family
  • Initially a poet, later burned his poems after meeting Socrates
  • Dedicated his life to questions of virtue and noble character
  • Used dialogue and debate for philosophical enquiry

docs.title: Core Philosophy: Knowledge Within
docs.text:
Unlike Locke, Plato believed that all knowledge is already present in the learner's mind, deeply hidden. Teaching is about helping students discover this knowledge themselves.

"By turning the eyes from looking in the wrong direction to the way it ought to be, one can observe everything correctly."

docs.title: The Dialectical Method
docs.text: Key techniques include: - Questioning - To stimulate thinking - Discussion - To explore ideas - Logical Arguments - To test validity - Analysis - To break down concepts - Inductive Reasoning - To draw conclusions

docs.title: Steps in Plato's Teaching Method
docs.text:
Step 1: Test Previous Knowledge
    │   (Through questioning)
    ▼
Step 2: Identify Elements
    │   (Help students find components of concept)
    ▼
Step 3: Classification & Categorization
    │   (Organize identified elements)
    ▼
Step 4: Higher-Order Thinking
        • Finding relationships between concepts
        • Combining known concepts to discover new ones
        • Drawing generalizations

docs.title: Teacher's Role in Plato's Model
docs.text:
The teacher does NOT act as the "all-knowing" authority. Instead:

  • Participates alongside students in the learning process
  • Moderates discussions and debates
  • Demands evidence for arguments from all sides
  • Collaborates with students to arrive at truth

Key Insight

This process helps BOTH students gain real knowledge AND teachers update their own understanding!

docs.title: 4.06.3 Immanuel Kant's Rule Model
docs.text:
About Immanuel Kant (1724-1804)

  • Famous German philosopher
  • Advocated that only through reasoning can we acquire real knowledge
  • Emphasized interrogation and inquiry in classroom instruction

docs.title: Core Philosophy: Rule-Based Learning
docs.text: Kant believed solutions to problems are found through reasoning by: - Reorganizing known facts - Combining ideas in new ways - Developing rules that govern known facts

docs.title: Inductive Reasoning (Specific → General)
docs.text:
Moving from individual observations to general principles:

Observation 1: Dilute Sulphuric acid + Zinc → Zinc Sulphate + Hydrogen↑
Observation 2: Dilute Nitric acid + Copper → Cupric Nitrate + Hydrogen↑
Observation 3: Dilute Hydrochloric acid + Silver → Silver chloride + Hydrogen↑
                                    ↓
        GENERAL PRINCIPLE: All metals react with dilute 
        inorganic acids to liberate hydrogen

docs.title: Deductive Reasoning (General → Specific)
docs.text:
Testing the general principle in specific instances:

General Principle: All metals + dilute acids → liberate Hydrogen
                                    ↓
        Test Case: Mercury + Hydrochloric acid → Hydrogen↑
                                    ↓
        Result: Principle VERIFIED!

docs.title: Practical Example: Finding Plurals in English
docs.text:
Step 1: Inductive Rule Development 

Boy → Boys       Orange → Oranges
Girl → Girls     Cycle → Cycles
Car → Cars       Tin → Tins

RULE: Add 's' to make singular nouns plural

Step 2: Testing the Rule 

Focus, Radius, Stimulus (words ending in 'us')
Adding 's' doesn't work here!

NEW RULE NEEDED: Replace 'us' with 'i'
Focus → Foci
Radius → Radii
Stimulus → Stimuli

Kant's Teaching Approach

  • Subject content is taught through rule-building and testing
  • Goal: Develop logical reasoning ability in students
  • All teaching components follow specific rules

docs.title: 4.07 Psychological Teaching Models
docs.text: These models are based on important psychological principles: - Reinforcement - Feedback - Systems approach - Classroom interaction analysis - Motivation techniques

docs.title: 4.07.1 Glaser's Basic Teaching Model
docs.text: This is considered the foundational model of teaching. DeCecco and Crawford regard it as the basic teaching model.

docs.title: Component Details
docs.text:
Component Description Instructional Objectives What students should attain upon completion; defined as observable behavioural outcomes Entering Behaviour Student's level before instruction begins - prior knowledge, intellectual ability, motivation, social/cultural factors Instructional Procedures The actual teaching process; how content is delivered; where most teacher decisions are made Performance Assessment Tests and observations to measure achievement of objectives

B.Ed. Lesson Plan Connection

This is exactly how B.Ed. students prepare their lesson plans:

  1. Instructional Objectives - Written in terms of pupil behaviour
  2. Previous Knowledge - Entry behaviour assessment
  3. Body of Lesson Plan (4 columns):
  4. Expected pupil behaviour
  5. Content/concept to be taught
  6. Learning experiences and materials
  7. Formative evaluation
  8. Review & Assignment - Summative evaluation

docs.title: 4.07.2 Flander's Interaction Analysis Model
docs.text: This model helps assess and improve teaching through systematic observation of classroom interactions.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
• Gage (1968) analyzed teaching and identified teaching skills as methods and techniques used in classroom instruction
  • B.K. Passi (1976) identified 14 micro-skills in classroom teaching through analysis of verbal and non-verbal behaviours

docs.title: Teacher Talk - Indirect Influence (Categories 1-4)
docs.text:
Encourages student participation and freedom of action

Category Behaviour 1 Accepts feelings of pupils (in an unthreatening manner) 2 Praises or encourages (jokes to release tension, nods, says "go on") 3 Accepts or uses ideas of pupils (clarifies, builds on student ideas) 4 Asks questions (with intent that students answer)

docs.title: Teacher Talk - Direct Influence (Categories 5-7)
docs.text:
Increases teacher control, aims at conformity and compliance

Category Behaviour 5 Lectures (gives facts, opinions, expresses own ideas, rhetorical questions) 6 Gives directions (commands, orders, expects compliance) 7 Criticizes or justifies authority (shouting, extreme self-reference)

docs.title: Student Talk (Categories 8-9)
docs.text: Category Behaviour 8 Student talk - Response (replies to teacher's questions) 9 Student talk - Initiation (student initiates the talk)

docs.title: Silence (Category 10)
docs.text: Category Behaviour 10 Silence or confusion (pauses, short periods of silence, noisy behaviour)

docs.title: How to Use FIAS
docs.text:
Step 1: Observation - Sit where you can see and hear all participants - Allow 5-10 minutes to get acclimatized - Record the category number every 3-5 seconds

Step 2: Create the Interaction Matrix - Add '10' at beginning and end of recorded numbers - Convert numbers into successive pairs - Plot pairs on a 10×10 matrix

Step 3: Calculate Behaviour Ratios

The 12 Key Ratios:

Ratio Formula What It Measures TTR (Teacher Talk Ratio) Σf[col 1-7]/N × 100 Teacher-based activities PTR (Pupil Talk Ratio) Σf[col 8-9]/N × 100 Student participation SCR (Silence/Confusion Ratio) Σf[col 10]/N × 100 Dead time/confusion CCR (Content Cross Ratio) Σf[col 4-5]/N × 100 Content presentation style I/D (Indirect/Direct Ratio) Σf[col 1-4]/Σf[col 5-7] × 100 Teaching style balance TRR (Teacher Response Ratio) Σf[col 1-3]/Σf[col 1-3,6-7] × 100 Acceptance of student ideas

docs.title: Using FIAS for Effective Teaching
docs.text:
Democratic Teacher (Uses categories 1,2,3,4 frequently)

  • Encourages student participation
  • Results in high learning proficiency
  • Creates an engaging classroom environment

Authoritative Teacher (Uses categories 5,6,7 frequently)

  • Gives more directions
  • Curtails student participation
  • Increases student dependence
  • Advised to change teaching style

Ineffective Communication (Frequent category 10)

  • Problems with verbal communication
  • Issues with classroom management
  • Needs significant improvement

docs.title: 4.07.3 Daniel Davies & Stolurow's Computer-Based Teaching Model
docs.text: This is the most complex teaching model, where the computer replaces the teacher in making decisions and providing instruction.

docs.title: Comparison with Glaser's Model
docs.text: Computer Model Phase Glaser's Model Components Pre-Tutorial Phase Instructional Objectives + Entering Behaviour + Instructional Procedures Tutorial Phase (Teacher Function) Instructional Procedures Tutorial Phase (Professor Function) Performance Assessment

docs.title: Advantages Over Conventional Instruction
docs.text:
Conventional Teaching Computer-Based Model Teacher makes all decisions Computer makes decisions Usually only one programme available Access to multiple alternative programmes Limited knowledge store Access to vast store of knowledge Decisions may be inconsistent Consistent, optimized decisions

Davies & Stolurow's View

"Only computers have the capacity to make all the decisions and accommodations an enlightened pedagogy requires."

docs.title: 4.08 Modern Teaching Models
docs.text: These models have different standpoints about educational goals and teaching methods. Joyce and Weil's classification is considered the most important, dividing them into four categories:

docs.title: 4.08.1 Information Processing Models
docs.text: These models focus on intellectual development and help students develop: - Creativity - Logical thinking - Analyzing and organizing information - Memory retention

docs.title: Key Information Processing Models
docs.text: Model Exponent(s) Primary Goals Inductive Reasoning Model Hilda Taba Developing inductive reasoning and logical analysis Enquiry Training Model Richard Suchman Training in systematic inquiry Science Enquiry Model Joseph J. Schwab Teaching research methods in a discipline Concept Attainment Model Jerome Bruner Developing inductive reasoning and concept formation Cognitive Development Model Jean Piaget, Irving Sigal, Edmund Sullivan Improving intellectual development, especially logical reasoning Advanced Organizer Model David Ausubel Increasing information processing efficiency; connecting new information to existing knowledge

docs.title: 4.08.2 Social Interaction Models
docs.text:
These models emphasize: - Personal and social relations - Ability to integrate with others - Functioning harmoniously in social groups - Democratic practices in the classroom

Guiding Principle

"All education is socialization"

docs.title: Key Social Interaction Models
docs.text: Model Exponent(s) Primary Goals Group Interaction Model Herbert Thelen, John Dewey Democratic participation skills + academic inquiry Classroom Meeting Model Glaser Self-understanding and social responsibility Social Inquiry Model Byron Massials, Benjamin Cox Solving social problems through academic inquiry Laboratory Model National Training Laboratory Self-awareness and flexibility through group skills Jurisprudent Model Donald Oliver, James P. Shaver Studying social problems legally Role Playing Model Frennie & George Shaftel Inquiring personal and social values Social Simulation Model Sarene Borock Experiencing social processes and examining reactions

docs.title: Steps in Implementing Social Interaction Model
docs.text:
Step 1: Teacher introduces topic and concept outline
                    ↓
Step 2: Students form teams (5-6 members each)
                    ↓
Step 3: Team members discuss in pairs/sub-groups
        • Negotiate and compromise
        • Explain concepts to each other
        • Consult other sub-groups if needed
                    ↓
Step 4: Teams assess their completion status
                    ↓
Step 5: Team representatives present findings to class
                    ↓
Step 6: Teacher completes left-out facts and concepts

Key Features

  • Student-to-student interactions are central
  • Students act as both facilitators and learners
  • Develops team working skills: compromise, negotiation, motivation
  • Teacher monitors to keep teams on task

docs.title: 4.08.3 Personal Development Models
docs.text: These models prioritize the affective domain (emotions, attitudes, values) and emphasize: - Positive relationships with environment - Unique individuality development - Personal goal realization - Self-esteem and self-efficacy - Understanding oneself and one's feelings

docs.title: Key Personal Development Models
docs.text: Model Exponent(s) Primary Goals Non-directive Model Carl Rogers Self-awareness, self-concept, autonomy Awareness Training Model Fritz Perls Interpersonal awareness, physical/sensory awareness Synectics Model William Gordon Creativity and innovative problem-solving Conceptual System Model David Hunt Personal competency and flexibility

docs.title: 4.08.4 Behaviour Modification Models
docs.text: Based on B.F. Skinner's behaviourism, these models focus on: - Modifying pupils' behaviour - Operant conditioning - shaping behaviour through reinforcement - Developing knowledge, abilities, attitudes, and skills

docs.title: Key Behaviour Modification Models
docs.text: Model Exponent(s) Primary Goals Conditioning Teaching Model B.F. Skinner Developing knowledge, abilities, attitudes, and skills through reinforcement Training Model B.F. Skinner Developing psychomotor skills and social skills

Key Takeaways

  1. Teaching models provide systematic frameworks for effective instruction
  2. All models share common elements: focus, syntax, principles of reaction, social system, support system, and application
  3. Philosophical models (Locke, Plato, Kant) address how knowledge is fundamentally acquired
  4. Psychological models (Glaser, Flanders, Davies) optimize the learning process through scientific analysis
  5. Modern models (Information Processing, Social Interaction, Personal Development, Behaviour Modification) address specific educational goals
  6. Effective teachers understand and apply multiple models based on context, objectives, and student needs

docs.text:
